description: Inositol phosphate metabolism generates and recycles the phosphorylated inositol species that mark membranes for identity and release calcium-mobilising second messengers. Its outputs govern how vesicles are sorted, how endosomes and autophagosomes mature, and how receptor signalling is terminated, so cells depend on it for membrane traffic as much as for signal transduction. Lipid kinases such as PIK3C2A, the class III enzyme PIK3C3 and the 5-kinase PIKFYVE phosphorylate inositol head groups on endosomal and autophagic membranes, while the polyphosphoinositide phosphatase synaptojanin removes phosphates to drive clathrin uncoating at synapses, and inositol monophosphatase completes the cycle by freeing myo-inositol for resynthesis. Loss of this turnover is damaging in neurons in particular: synaptojanin mutations cause parkinsonism and epileptic encephalopathy, and lithium acts partly by inhibiting the monophosphatase step.

A mixed immune-expression module centred on mononuclear leukocyte identity and trafficking, combining chemokine receptors, GTPase-of-immunity-associated proteins and transcriptional regulators. Monocyte and macrophage recruitment to inflamed tissue depends on CCR2 and CX3CR1, whose ligands direct patrolling and infiltrating cells to vessel walls and injured sites; loss of this axis blunts inflammatory monocyte egress from bone marrow and reshapes atherosclerotic and neuroinflammatory disease. The GIMAP proteins act in lymphocyte survival and homeostasis, linking the set to T cell persistence as well as myeloid function. Signalling and feedback components include the IL-1 receptor accessory protein required for interleukin-1 responses, the MAPK phosphatase DUSP4 that dampens kinase output, the TNF-family receptor FN14, and the immediate-early factor NR4A3. Numerous KRAB-type zinc finger proteins and the repressor HIC1 suggest accompanying transcriptional control, alongside metabolic and autophagy-related members.

Rho family GTPases switch between GDP- and GTP-bound states, and the cycling itself — loading by exchange factors, inactivation by GTPase-activating proteins — is what converts signals into localized actomyosin contraction. The genes here tie that cycle to cell division: ECT2 is the exchange factor that activates RhoA at the equatorial cortex, while RACGAP1, its partner in the centralspindlin complex, provides GAP activity and helps position the cleavage furrow. PRC1 crosslinks antiparallel midzone microtubules and CEP55 recruits abscission machinery to the midbody, so the pathway spans furrow ingression through the final severing of the daughter cells. Several ARHGAP and DEPDC1 members add further inactivating or regulatory input, and E2F2 links the whole programme to S-phase entry. Loss of control here produces failed cytokinesis, binucleate cells and aneuploidy, and these genes are recurrently overexpressed in proliferative tumours.

Somatic cells duplicate their chromosomes and partition them equally into two daughters, and this mitotic cell cycle module covers the commitment to division and the machinery that executes it. Getting it wrong produces aneuploidy, tetraploidy and the chromosomal instability that characterises tumours; sustained overexpression of these genes is one of the most consistent proliferation signatures in cancer tissue. Mitotic cyclins partnered with CDK1 drive entry into mitosis, opposed by the inhibitory kinases WEE1-family member PKMYT1 and reversed by CDC25 phosphatases that remove the restraining phosphates. FOXM1 supplies the transcriptional programme for the G2/M genes. Downstream, PLK1 and NEK2 coordinate spindle assembly and centrosome separation, PLK4 and centriolar proteins such as CEP152 license centriole duplication, gamma-tubulin nucleates microtubules, and shugoshin protects centromeric cohesion until anaphase.

Cells attach to each other and to the matrix around them, and this cell adhesion programme supplies both the ligands and the receptors that make those contacts. It underlies tissue architecture, wound healing, leukocyte recruitment and platelet plug formation, and its dysregulation contributes to fibrosis, thrombosis and tumour invasion. Fibrillar and network collagens together with fibronectin, laminins, nidogen, tenascin, periostin and thrombospondins build the adhesive substrate, while integrins such as the platelet fibrinogen receptor pair ITGA2B/ITGB3, the von Willebrand factor receptor complex GP1BA/GP9, and endothelial adhesion molecules VCAM1, SELP and junctional JAM3/ESAM mediate binding under flow. Chemokines CXCL12 and IL8 and the cytokine IL1B activate these receptors on circulating cells, and SNAI2 links the same machinery to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, coupling adhesion to migration and matrix remodelling.

These genes mark the differentiated tissue macrophage and microglial state, the resident phagocyte programme that clears debris and dying cells, handles iron and heme, and shapes local immune tone. Fc receptor gamma chain and the Tec kinase BTK couple immunoglobulin and immune-complex recognition to phagocytosis, while CYBB encodes the NADPH oxidase catalytic subunit gp91phox that generates the respiratory burst; its loss causes chronic granulomatous disease with recurrent bacterial and fungal infection. Heme oxygenase-1 degrades heme to biliverdin, carbon monoxide and free iron, linking these cells to erythrocyte recycling and to copper and amino acid transport by SLC31A2 and SLC7A7. IDO1 with KMO and KYNU carries tryptophan down the kynurenine route, producing metabolites that suppress T cell responses and, in brain, act on neurons. MAFB sustains the macrophage identity underlying all of it.

This grouping captures the transcriptional signature of mature B cells, the antibody-producing lineage of adaptive immunity, and its members are the surface proteins by which B cells are recognised and therapeutically targeted. The core is the antigen receptor complex and its immediate modulators: CD79A and CD79B transmit immunoglobulin engagement into intracellular signalling, while CD19 amplifies that signal and CD22, CD72 and BTLA restrain it, setting the threshold at which a B cell responds to antigen rather than ignoring it or reacting to self. Complement receptor CR2 links innate opsonisation to B cell activation, CXCR5 directs homing into follicles and germinal centres, and HLA-DOB tunes peptide loading for presentation to helper T cells. MS4A1, the CD20 target of depleting antibodies, and Fc receptor-like proteins complete a profile that distinguishes B cells in tissue and blood expression data.

A mixed group of broadly expressed regulators that keep housekeeping functions of the cell running: chromatin-associated and transcriptional components, RNA-binding proteins, and machinery for endosomal membrane traffic and cytoskeletal contractility. Several members act on gene expression — a chromatin-interacting subunit of a histone deacetylase-containing repressor complex, a cyclin partner of the CDK8 kinase module of Mediator, and the zinc-finger transcription factor SP3. Others control the fate of mRNAs after they are made: MBNL1 governs alternative splicing of muscle and neuronal transcripts, FMR1 represses translation at synapses and its loss causes fragile X syndrome, and G3BP2 nucleates stress granules when translation stalls. A third arm handles membranes and organelles, including the ESCRT-associated ATPase VPS4B in multivesicular body formation, a phosphoinositide phosphatase acting at the Golgi and ER, and a myosin phosphatase targeting subunit that tunes actomyosin tension.

This module marks the professional antigen-presenting compartment of the immune system, where extracellular proteins are displayed on MHC class II to CD4 T cells so that helper responses, antibody production and immunological memory can be initiated. Its core is the class II locus itself — HLA-DR alpha and beta chains together with the HLA-DM chaperone that catalyses exchange of the invariant chain-derived placeholder peptide for high-affinity antigenic peptides in the late endosome. Around this sit the adhesion and signalling components that make a productive contact with the T cell and sustain it: ICAM1 with the integrin beta-2 chain, the pan-leukocyte phosphatase CD45, CD53, and the myeloid adaptors AIF1, FYB and PLEK. Expression of this programme in monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells defines their competence to present; loss of class II expression causes profound combined immunodeficiency, while its inappropriate induction contributes to autoimmunity and transplant rejection.

Myeloid dendritic cells only present antigen usefully if they can leave the tissue where they captured it and find the T cell zones of a draining lymph node, and this directed migration is what the chemotaxis programme provides. Stromal and lymphatic endothelial cells lay down the chemokines CCL19 and CCL21, which the receptor CCR7 reads on the maturing dendritic cell surface, converting a gradient into polarized crawling toward and along lymphatic vessels. Downstream, a Rho-family guanine nucleotide exchange factor couples that signal to cytoskeletal rearrangement, while the myeloid transcription factor PU.1 specifies the cell type in which this machinery is expressed. Loss of the receptor or its ligands strands antigen-loaded cells in the periphery, blunting priming of naive T cells and tolerance induction; the same axis is exploited by tumour cells for nodal metastasis.

As a replication fork passes, the DNA it leaves behind must be repackaged into nucleosomes within minutes, and replication-dependent chromatin assembly is the machinery that does it. Without it, newly copied DNA stays naked and vulnerable, forks stall, and the epigenetic state of the parent chromatin is not restored in the daughter cells. Histone H3-H4 dimers are escorted from their point of synthesis by soluble chaperones, handed to ASF1A and ASF1B, and delivered to the CAF-1 complex, whose CHAF1A and CHAF1B subunits are recruited to the fork through PCNA and deposit the H3-H4 tetramer onto nascent DNA before H2A-H2B completes the particle. RBBP4 links this histone handling to chromatin-modifying and remodelling complexes that mature the new nucleosomes. The result couples S-phase histone supply to DNA synthesis and underlies heritable chromatin organisation and genome stability.

Sugars attached to serine, threonine, tyrosine or hydroxylysine side chains give secreted and membrane proteins their bulk, charge and binding specificity, and protein O-linked glycosylation covers all of the routes by which these chains are initiated and extended. Mucin-type synthesis begins with a large family of polypeptide GalNAc transferases and the core-1 galactosyltransferase with its chaperone, then branches, sialylates and fucosylates to build selectin ligands and mucus barriers. Separate arms make O-mannose glycans on dystroglycan, whose loss causes congenital muscular dystrophy with brain and eye involvement; O-fucose and O-glucose on EGF repeats, which tune Notch; collagen galactosyl-hydroxylysine; and the xylose-primed linker that nucleates heparan and chondroitin sulfate chains, with sulfotransferases and epimerases setting their sulfation patterns. Nucleotide-sugar transporters and the nucleocytoplasmic O-GlcNAc cycle of OGT and OGA complete the picture, linking nutrient status to signalling.

Tyrosine catabolism disposes of the aromatic amino acid taken in from diet and protein turnover, converting it in the liver and kidney to fumarate and acetoacetate that feed the citric acid cycle and ketogenesis. The route runs through transamination to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate by tyrosine aminotransferase, dioxygenase-mediated conversion to homogentisate by HPD, ring cleavage by homogentisate dioxygenase, isomerization by the maleylacetoacetate isomerase activity of GSTZ1, and final hydrolysis by fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase. Blocks at each step cause recognizable inherited disease: HPD or FAH deficiency gives tyrosinemia with hepatorenal damage from accumulated reactive intermediates, while loss of homogentisate dioxygenase causes alkaptonuria, in which homogentisate polymerizes and pigments cartilage. IL4I1, an L-amino acid oxidase secreted by myeloid cells, oxidizes tyrosine and other aromatic amino acids in the immune microenvironment rather than for energy, linking this chemistry to local amino acid depletion and T cell suppression.

Whether a muscle cell contracts, how strongly and how fast, is set by processes that tune calcium delivery to the sarcomere and the sensitivity of the sarcomere to it; this regulation of muscle contraction covers cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle alike. It determines cardiac output and rhythm, vascular tone and blood pressure, gut and airway motility, and skeletal muscle force, and its failure produces arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, malignant hyperthermia-type disorders and hypertension. Voltage-gated calcium and sodium channels, potassium and pacemaker channels, and the sarcoplasmic reticulum release and uptake machinery (ryanodine receptors, SERCA pumps with phospholamban, calsequestrin, triadin and junctophilins) shape the calcium transient, while troponins, tropomyosin, myosin light chains and their kinases translate it into force. Layered on top are G protein-coupled inputs from adrenergic, muscarinic, endothelin, purinergic and tachykinin receptors acting through cyclic nucleotides, calmodulin and RhoA, plus transcriptional and microRNA control of the contractile programme.

The inner mitochondrial membrane is folded into cristae, and the shaping and maintenance of that architecture is what this pathway describes. Cristae geometry sets how densely respiratory complexes can pack, how much cytochrome c is sequestered, and therefore how much ATP a cell makes and how readily it commits to apoptosis; its collapse underlies optic atrophy, cardiomyopathy and mitochondrial encephalopathy. Central to it is the MICOS complex at cristae junctions, built around mitofilin (IMMT) with CHCHD3, CHCHD6, APOO and APOOL, tethered to the outer membrane through SAMM50 and the metaxins. OPA1 controls inner membrane fusion and junction tightness and is cleaved by the stress proteases OMA1 and AFG3L2. Carrier-pathway TIM chaperones and the insertases OXA1L and COX18 deliver membrane proteins into the bilayer, while tafazzin remodels cardiolipin, the lipid that stabilises the curvature these proteins impose.

Sensory perception covers the machinery by which the nervous system captures a physical or chemical stimulus, transduces it into an electrical signal, and encodes its quality and intensity. The gene list spans the major modalities: visual phototransduction through rhodopsin and cone opsins, transducin, cGMP phosphodiesterase subunits, cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and the retinoid cycle enzymes that regenerate chromophore; a very large olfactory receptor repertoire with its trafficking cofactors and the vomeronasal and trace-amine receptors; sweet, umami and bitter taste receptors coupled to gustducin and PLC signalling; hair-cell mechanotransduction and stereocilia architecture via myosins, cadherin 23, protocadherin 15, usherin and whirlin; and somatosensory channels such as TRPV1, TRPM8, PIEZO2 and sensory sodium channels for pain, temperature and touch. Also present are lens crystallins and eye and ear developmental transcription factors. Failure of these components produces retinal degeneration, inherited deafness, cataract, anosmia and congenital insensitivity to pain.

Skeletal muscle repairs itself by fusing mononucleate myoblasts, derived from activated satellite cells, either into damaged fibres or with one another to build new multinucleate myotubes; this fusion step is what restores contractile mass after injury and what fails in ageing muscle and dystrophic disease, where regeneration cannot keep pace with damage. Membrane fusion here is driven by dedicated muscle-specific micropeptides: myomaker, a multipass membrane protein required for fusogenicity, acts together with the small myomerger protein to bring apposed myoblast membranes past hemifusion. The tetraspanins CD9 and CD81, with their partner PTGFRN, organize the membrane microdomains in which fusion and adhesion occur. Loss of the fusogens leaves myoblasts able to differentiate but unable to form multinucleated fibres, separating fusion from myogenic commitment as a distinct, genetically controlled stage of regeneration.

Microautophagy delivers cytosolic material into the lumen of late endosomes or lysosomes without building a separate autophagosome: the limiting membrane of the degradative compartment invaginates directly, pinches off, and the cargo is degraded still wrapped in a single membrane derived from that invagination. It provides a route for turnover of proteins and portions of cytoplasm, and for remodelling the lysosomal membrane itself, complementing the larger-scale macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated uptake pathways in maintaining protein and organelle quality control. The machinery overlaps heavily with canonical autophagy: the ULK1/ULK2 initiation kinases with ATG13 and RB1CC1, the ATG12–ATG5–ATG16L1 conjugation system with the E1-like enzyme ATG7, ATG4 proteases that process and delipidate ATG8-family proteins, lipid-transfer proteins ATG2A/ATG2B and the transmembrane lipid scramblase ATG9A. Membrane scission draws on the ESCRT-associated AAA-ATPases VPS4A and VPS4B, and sorting nexins contribute membrane recognition.

Adding a phosphate to a threonine residue in a protein is one of the basic switches cells use to change enzyme activity, protein interactions and localisation on a fast timescale. Peptidyl-threonine phosphorylation gathers the kinases and regulators that carry out and control this modification, and through it cell cycle progression, stress responses, growth factor signalling and ion transport are all set. The genes span several kinase families: cyclin-dependent kinases and the checkpoint kinase CHEK1 that time mitotic entry and arrest damaged cells, AKT1 and MAPK1/MAPK8 acting downstream of growth factor and stress inputs, the LKB1 kinase STK11 in energy sensing, WNK3 and STK39 in regulating cation-chloride cotransporters, and TBK1 in innate immune signalling. Substrates include transcription factors such as ATF2, linking threonine phosphorylation to changes in gene expression. Misregulation of these kinases underlies tumour growth, hypertension and impaired damage responses.

Extending a DNA strand by adding nucleotides to its 3' end is the productive step of replication, and the machinery here covers both the polymerases that do it and the factors that keep forks moving through chromatin. Without it cells cannot duplicate their genomes on schedule, and stalled or collapsed forks become the source of the chromosomal breaks and rearrangements that drive cancer. Replicative polymerases alpha, delta and epsilon work behind an MCM helicase and GINS, with PCNA as the sliding clamp loaded by RFC subunits, DNA2 and LIG1 processing and sealing Okazaki fragments. The INO80 chromatin remodelling complex, with its RUVBL1/RUVBL2 ATPases, clears nucleosomes ahead of the fork and aids restart. MRE11-RAD50-NBN handles damaged forks, while TERT and POT1 extend and protect the chromosome ends that conventional elongation cannot finish.

Bone morphogenetic protein signals instruct skeletal patterning, joint formation, vascular development and iron homeostasis, and the cell must be able to switch them off with precision; negative regulation of the BMP signaling pathway is the collection of brakes that sets how much ligand reaches a receptor and how long the response lasts. Secreted antagonists such as noggin, chordin, gremlins, twisted gastrulation and sclerostin sequester ligands extracellularly, while a pseudoreceptor and BMPER tune receptor availability at the cell surface. Inside the cell, inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7 recruit the SMURF ubiquitin ligases to degrade receptors and effectors, phosphatases reverse SMAD activation, and SKI/SKIL and TOB1 silence SMAD-driven transcription; numerous microRNAs damp component expression. Loss of these restraints produces heterotopic ossification and sclerosing bone disease, and the hepcidin-regulating arm involving hemojuvelin, erythroferrone and TMPRSS6 links the same brakes to systemic iron loading.

Epithelia line every body surface and duct, and this pathway covers how an unspecialized progenitor takes on epithelial identity: apical-basal polarity, junctional sealing, and the terminal specializations of skin, gut, kidney, airway, lens, hair and inner ear. Its outputs are the barrier that keeps water in and microbes out, the absorptive and secretory surfaces of the viscera, and the ciliated and sensory epithelia; failure produces ichthyosis and other cornification disorders, ciliopathies, deafness, cataract and loss of the differentiation controls whose collapse underlies carcinoma and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Lineage transcription factors such as GRHL2, KLF4, FOXA1, CDX2 and OVOL family members act downstream of Wnt, BMP/TGF-beta, Notch, Hedgehog and Hippo cues, driving keratin, small proline-rich and late cornified envelope genes, transglutaminase crosslinking, claudin and tight-junction assembly, and cell-cycle exit through CDKN1A and CDKN1B.

Myosin filament organization covers the assembly, arrangement and disassembly of the thick filaments built from myosin molecules, the motor structures that generate contractile force in muscle and in non-muscle cells. Correct thick filament geometry sets sarcomere length, the register of myosin heads against actin, and thus the force a cell can produce; disruption underlies cardiomyopathies and myopathies as well as defects in smooth muscle tone. Titin, the giant elastic sarcomeric protein, and its Z-disc partner telethonin template and stabilize filament arrangement and provide passive stiffness, while smooth muscle myosin heavy chain supplies the filament subunit itself. A kinase acting on myosin regulatory light chain links signalling to filament activation and contractility, connecting this structural biology to cytoskeletal remodelling, cell shape change and vascular and visceral smooth muscle function.

TOR signaling is the cell's master decision point on whether conditions favour growth: the mTOR kinase integrates amino acid supply, glucose and energy status, oxygen and growth factor input, and converts a favourable verdict into protein synthesis, lipid and nucleotide production, and suppression of autophagy. Two complexes carry the output, one built on RPTOR that phosphorylates S6 kinases and the 4E-BP translation repressors, the other on RICTOR. Amino acids are sensed at the lysosome, where the Ragulator scaffold and Rag GTPases position the kinase, with GATOR components, FLCN and sensors such as CASTOR1 and SAMTOR tuning the response; the TSC1/TSC2 complex acts as a GTPase-activating protein toward RHEB, and AMPK and LKB1 impose energy restraint. Loss of these brakes causes tuberous sclerosis and related hamartoma syndromes, and pathway hyperactivation is common in cancer, epilepsy and metabolic disease.

Cells that meet a microbe, an injury or a chemotactic gradient must not only detect it but amplify the reaction, and this collection of positive regulators of the response to external stimuli is what raises the gain. It underpins innate immune defence, inflammation, wound healing and leukocyte recruitment, and its over-activity produces septic shock, autoinflammatory fever syndromes and chronic inflammatory disease. Pattern-recognition receptors of the Toll-like, NOD-like and RIG-I-like families feed through adaptors such as MYD88, TICAM1, MAVS and STING1 into IRAK and TBK1 kinases, NF-kB and interferon-regulatory factors, while inflammasome components including NLRP3, PYCARD and CASP1 mature IL-1B and IL-18 and drive gasdermin-mediated lytic death. Complement factors, ficolins, chemokines and their receptors, growth factors, coagulation proteins and many ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases and microRNAs tune the strength and duration of the response.

Gonadotropin secretion is the regulated release of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone from pituitary gonadotropes, the step that drives ovarian follicle maturation, ovulation, spermatogenesis and gonadal steroid output; its failure produces hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, delayed or absent puberty and infertility. Hypothalamic input dominates the control: kisspeptin and neurokinin B acting through their receptors, together with opioid and RFamide-related signals, shape pulsatile GnRH release, which the gonadotrope reads through its GnRH receptor. Feedback from the gonads arrives as activin and inhibin subunits signalling through SMAD-dependent transcription, selectively tuning FSH beta relative to the shared glycoprotein alpha subunit. Metabolic and stress cues enter through leptin and corticotropin-releasing hormone, linking reproductive competence to energy stores. Transcription factors including FOXL2 and TBX3 establish and maintain the gonadotrope and hypothalamic cell identities on which this endocrine axis depends.

Signalling receptors are not permanent fixtures; their degradation sets how long and how strongly a cell can respond to a hormone, growth factor or ligand. This receptor catabolic process covers the routes by which receptors are marked, internalised and destroyed, chiefly ubiquitin-dependent sorting into lysosomes. HECT-domain and RING ligases such as NEDD4, NEDD4L, ITCH, SMURF1 and the Wnt-receptor ligases RNF43 and ZNRF3 tag receptors for downregulation, while MYLIP targets the LDL receptor and secreted PCSK9 drives its lysosomal disposal, a link that underlies cholesterol handling and lipid-lowering therapy. Endosomal and autophagy machinery -- BECN1, UVRAG, PIK3R4, KIF16B and ESCRT-associated MVB12A -- delivers cargo onward, and lysosomal proteases including legumain complete breakdown. Loss of this turnover leaves receptors signalling unchecked, a route to hyperproliferation, and also governs iron control through hepcidin-driven ferroportin loss.

Integrins must be switched from a low- to a high-affinity state before a cell can grip the extracellular matrix or another cell, and this pathway covers the inputs that push them in that direction. Strengthened integrin-mediated adhesion underlies platelet aggregation and clot stability, leukocyte arrest on endothelium and migration into lymphoid tissue, and the traction cells need for spreading and matrix remodelling. Kindlin-1 and CIB1 act at the integrin cytoplasmic tail to promote activation, focal adhesion kinase and RAC3 couple engaged receptors to cytoskeletal assembly, and in immune cells SYK, SKAP1 and the phosphatase PTPN6 tune signalling from antigen and chemokine receptors such that adhesion follows activation. Chemokines, TGF-beta family ligands and mechanical force sensed through PIEZO1 provide upstream cues, linking adhesion strength to inflammation, haemostasis and tissue mechanics.

High-density lipoprotein particles are not static cargo containers; they are continuously rebuilt as they circulate, and this remodeling sets how much cholesterol they can carry back from tissues to the liver. It underlies reverse cholesterol transport and is the biology behind HDL cholesterol as a cardiovascular risk marker. Nascent discoidal particles built on apolipoprotein A-I acquire cell-derived cholesterol via ABCG1, and LCAT esterifies it to form a hydrophobic core and a mature spherical particle. CETP then exchanges cholesteryl ester for triglyceride with apoB-containing lipoproteins, hepatic and endothelial lipases hydrolyse core and surface lipids to shrink particles, phospholipid transfer protein shuffles surface phospholipid, and SCARB1 delivers cholesteryl ester to hepatocytes and steroidogenic cells. Exchangeable apolipoproteins such as APOA2, APOC3, APOE and APOM determine particle composition and enzyme access; their imbalance produces dyslipidaemia and atherosclerosis.

Erythropoietin is the kidney-derived hormone that tells red cell progenitors to survive, divide and mature, and the cellular reactions to it set the rate of erythropoiesis and thus blood oxygen-carrying capacity. Loss of the response causes anaemia, as in renal failure, while constitutive activation of its signalling drives polycythaemia and myeloproliferative disease. The hormone binds a dedicated receptor whose dimerisation activates the receptor-associated kinase JAK2; phosphorylated STAT5 then enters the nucleus to switch on anti-apoptotic and differentiation genes, with CREB1 contributing further transcriptional output. An erythroid-specific JAK2 substrate, RHEX, and cooperation with stem cell factor signalling through KIT amplify progenitor expansion. Induction of metallothioneins reflects the accompanying handling of metal and oxidative stress in maturing erythroblasts, linking this hormonal axis to iron and redox physiology.

Midbrain dopaminergic neurons must send axons along stereotyped routes to the striatum and prefrontal cortex, and dopaminergic neuron axon guidance is the steering process that gets them there. The accuracy of this wiring sets the anatomy of the nigrostriatal and mesolimbic systems that control voluntary movement, motivation and reward; mistargeting leaves dopamine release in the wrong place and is a plausible developmental contributor to motor and psychiatric dysfunction. The cues here are Wnt ligands acting through non-canonical, planar-cell-polarity-type receiving machinery: a Frizzled receptor together with the atypical cadherin CELSR3, the core polarity protein VANGL2, and the atypical tyrosine kinase receptor RYK, which reads Wnt gradients as attractive or repulsive instructions at the growth cone. Signalling converges on cytoskeletal remodelling and oriented outgrowth, linking this pathway to the broader use of polarity proteins in axon tract formation.

Cells with identical genomes maintain different expression programmes because chromatin itself carries heritable information, and this is the machinery that writes, reads, erases and propagates it. Such epigenetic regulation of gene expression establishes lineage identity, silences repetitive and parasitic DNA, imprints maternal and paternal alleles, inactivates one X chromosome, and keeps the settings stable through rounds of DNA replication even after the initiating signal is gone. The components span DNA methylation writers and the TET dioxygenases that initiate demethylation, methyl-CpG readers such as MECP2 and UHRF1, histone acetyltransferases opposed by HDAC and sirtuin deacetylases, H3K9 and H3K27 methyltransferases with Polycomb and HP1 silencing complexes, ATP-dependent nucleosome remodellers, histone variants and linker histones, and a piRNA-guided arm that silences transposons in germ cells. Misdirection of these activities underlies imprinting disorders, Rett syndrome, and widespread silencing of tumour suppressors in cancer.

Hair grows only during anagen, the active phase of the hair cycle in which the follicle rebuilds its lower portion, the matrix proliferates, and a new shaft is produced and pushed outward; in human scalp hair this phase can last several years and so sets hair length. Entry into and maintenance of this phase depends on Wnt signalling to the follicular stem cell and dermal papilla compartments, with WNT10B and WNT5A acting as ligands and CTNNB1 as the transcriptional effector that drives hair placode and matrix fate. Adhesion and epidermal barrier components such as the focal adhesion protein FERMT1 and the protease inhibitor SPINK5 link follicle growth to the integrity of the surrounding epithelium. Failure of anagen entry, or premature exit into regression and rest, produces thinning and alopecia, while its dysregulation contributes to hair shaft and follicular malformations.

Damage-induced p53 signalling must be switched off once repair is complete, and damping of this DNA damage response by p53-class mediators sets how readily a cell commits to arrest, senescence or apoptosis. The brake matters in both directions: too much restraint lets damaged cells proliferate and is a route to tumour formation, while too little causes excessive cell death and loss of stem and progenitor pools. MDM2 is the central ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for degradation and holds its level low in unstressed cells; SIRT1 deacetylates p53 to blunt its transcriptional output, and the demethylase KDM1A removes methyl marks that otherwise stabilise activated p53. DYRK-family kinases, the gankyrin proteasome regulator PSMD10, and the mesenchymal transcription factors SNAI1, SNAI2 and TWIST1 add further repression, linking p53 suppression to epithelial-mesenchymal transition and to signals from MIF and CD74.

Blood and lymphatic vessels are lined by a single sheet of flattened cells, and endothelial cell differentiation is how mesodermal, bone marrow or neural crest precursors acquire that identity. It determines whether vessels form at all, whether they become arterial, venous or lymphatic, and whether the barrier they present to blood is tight or leaky. Lineage specification runs through transcription factors such as ETV2, SOX17/SOX18, NR2F2 and PROX1, downstream of VEGFA signalling via KDR and NRP1, Notch-Delta/Jagged input with HEY1/HEY2, and BMP/TGF-beta receptors including ACVRL1, BMPR2 and SMAD4. Maturation brings the junctional and adhesion apparatus that defines the endothelium -- VE-cadherin, PECAM1, claudin-5 and the tight junction scaffolds -- plus Rap1 and Rho-kinase control of barrier tone and numerous microRNAs tuning the programme. Failure or corruption of these steps underlies cerebral cavernous malformation, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, and pathological angiogenesis in tumours.

GTP is both the nucleotide substrate for RNA synthesis and the switch that powers most molecular motors and signalling GTPases, so the reactions that make, interconvert and hydrolyse it set the pace for growth and intracellular traffic. Synthesis here runs through IMP dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting step of de novo guanine nucleotide production and the target of immunosuppressive drugs, while nucleoside diphosphate kinases of the NME family and adenylate kinase relatives phosphorylate GDP and balance nucleotide pools across cytosol and mitochondria. The consuming side is represented by hydrolases that use GTP to do work: RAN for nucleocytoplasmic transport, RAB and RHO family members for vesicle and cytoskeletal control, heterotrimeric G protein subunits for receptor signalling, and the mitochondrial dynamin-like proteins OPA1 and MFN1 for inner- and outer-membrane fusion. Depletion of guanine nucleotides therefore stalls proliferation, protein synthesis and organelle remodelling simultaneously.

Biological timekeeping lets cells and tissues anticipate the day rather than merely react to it, and this rhythmic process collection covers the generation and maintenance of such physiological rhythms — circadian cycles above all, plus ultradian and seasonal timing in the reproductive and somatic endocrine axes. Its core is a transcriptional feedback loop in which CLOCK and BMAL1 drive PER and CRY genes whose products feed back to shut down their own activators, with casein kinases, the FBXL3 substrate adaptor of a cullin-RING ligase, and deubiquitinases setting the roughly 24-hour period through timed protein degradation. Nuclear receptors such as REV-ERB and ROR family members, chromatin modifiers and SIRT1-linked metabolic sensors couple the clock to lipid and energy metabolism, while melatonin and non-visual opsin photoreceptors entrain it to light. Loss of this timing disrupts sleep, hormone release, and metabolic homeostasis.

Positive chemotaxis is the steering of a motile cell up a chemical gradient, and it underlies wound healing, angiogenesis, immune surveillance and axon guidance. Without accurate attraction, leukocytes fail to reach infected or injured tissue, new vessels do not sprout toward hypoxic regions, and growing axons miss their targets; the same cues are co-opted by tumour cells to invade and by leukocytes to sustain chronic inflammation. The attractants here span several families: chemokines such as CCL2, CCL5, CXCL12, CXCL8 and CX3CL1 acting on G protein-coupled receptors; VEGF family ligands with KDR and the co-receptor NRP1 drawing endothelial tip cells; HGF through MET and neurotrophic factors such as GDNF, ARTN and NTF3 guiding epithelial and neuronal migration; plus defensins, alarmins including HMGB1 and MIF, and formyl peptide sensing via FPR2. Downstream, cytoskeletal and polarity regulators including CORO1A and SCRIB convert the gradient into directed protrusion.

Touch, hearing, balance and mechanical pain all begin with a cell converting force into an electrical signal, and this is the transduction step of that sensory perception. Hair cells of the inner ear and mechanoreceptive and nociceptive neurons of the dorsal root ganglia depend on it; when it fails the result is deafness, vestibular dysfunction, loss of discriminative touch, or altered pain thresholds. Force-gated channels sit at the centre: PIEZO2 in light-touch and proprioceptive endings, TMC1 and TMC2 with the accessory subunits LHFPL5 and the tip-link and stereocilia proteins whorlin, stereocilin, PTPRQ and the very large adhesion GPCR ADGRV1 in cochlear hair bundles, alongside acid-sensing channels and TRPA1 in irritant and mechanical nociception. Voltage-gated sodium channels including SCN9A and SCN11A and potassium channels such as KCNQ1 and KCNK2 then shape the resulting receptor potential into propagated firing, with neurotrophin and transcriptional regulators supporting the sensory cells themselves.

Equal division of the genome requires that paired sister chromatids, held together from S phase onward, be released simultaneously and only after every chromosome is correctly attached to the spindle. Mitotic sister chromatid separation is that irreversible step, and errors in it produce aneuploid daughter cells, the chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours. Cohesin subunits such as RAD21 hold the pairs until separase (ESPL1) cleaves them, an event licensed by the anaphase-promoting complex and its activator CDC20 once securin/FBXO5 and cyclin B are destroyed. Until then, unattached kinetochores signal through the spindle assembly checkpoint / MAD1, MAD2, BUB1, BUB3, BUBR1 and the RZZ and dynein-dependent machinery / to sequester CDC20 and delay cleavage. The chromosomal passenger complex of Aurora B, INCENP and survivin, with Haspin and PLK1, corrects faulty attachments so that separation occurs only when biorientation is achieved.

Synaptic signalling is tuned as much by restraint as by release, and this grouping covers the processes that dampen neurotransmitter movement — both vesicular release at the terminal and carrier-mediated uptake or efflux. Such brakes set how much transmitter reaches receptors per stimulus and protect against excitotoxicity and runaway excitation; their loss is linked to movement disorders and neurodegeneration. Several members act directly at the release machinery: synaptotagmin-1 is the calcium sensor that triggers fusion, while synaptotagmin-11 and alpha-synuclein constrain exocytosis, and parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase mutated in recessive parkinsonism, regulates their abundance. Others impose modulatory control — nitric oxide produced by neuronal NOS acts as a diffusible retrograde signal, acid-sensing channels couple extracellular pH to terminal excitability, and PNKD variants cause paroxysmal dyskinesia. Together they place presynaptic gain control within broader regulation of neuronal communication and dopaminergic vulnerability.

Sodium is the dominant extracellular cation, and keeping its concentration within narrow limits sets cell volume, membrane excitability, extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure. Maintaining that steady state depends on transporters and on the hormones that tune them. The Na+/K+-ATPase catalytic and beta subunits, together with their FXYD regulators, establish the transmembrane gradient that all secondary sodium-coupled transport exploits; NHE-family exchangers couple sodium entry to proton extrusion and thus to intracellular pH, while NKCC and NCC cotransporters and the epithelial sodium channel subunits reabsorb filtered sodium along the nephron. Superimposed on this are the renin-angiotensin and aldosterone-synthesizing arms, natriuretic peptide signalling through its guanylate cyclase receptor, and endothelin, which respectively promote or oppose sodium retention. Disruption produces salt-sensitive hypertension, renal salt-wasting or pseudohypoaldosteronism, and, through the neuronal ATPase subunits, familial migraine and dystonia-parkinsonism.

SMAD proteins are the intracellular messengers of the TGF-beta, activin and BMP families, and this pathway covers everything that raises or lowers the strength and duration of that message. The set of controls matters because dose matters: the same ligands specify left-right asymmetry and mesoderm, drive bone and cartilage formation, restrain epithelial proliferation, and set vascular tone, so mistuning them produces skeletal dysplasias, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, fibrosis and tumour progression. Regulation acts at every level — secreted antagonists such as noggin, gremlin and twisted gastrulation sequester BMPs; co-receptors including endoglin and betaglycan alter ligand access to type I and type II serine/threonine kinase receptors; inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7 and repressors such as SKI and TOB1 damp receptor-activated SMAD complexes; and numerous microRNAs tune transcript levels of ligands, receptors and SMADs themselves. Iron sensing and unfolded-protein-response components also feed in.

The mammary ductal tree is built by branching morphogenesis, in which epithelial ducts elongate from the nipple through the fat pad and bifurcate to fill it, creating the architecture that later supports alveolar differentiation and milk delivery. Without it the gland remains rudimentary and cannot lactate; the same growth and branching controls, when deregulated, underlie much of breast cancer biology. Steroid hormone receptors for estrogen, progesterone, androgen and vitamin D read systemic endocrine cues and act largely through paracrine relays, with amphiregulin acting as the estrogen-induced signal from luminal cells to surrounding stroma. Macrophage and eosinophil recruitment via CSF1 and CCL11 supplies stromal support at the invading end buds, while WNT4 and WNT5A, TGFB1, receptor tyrosine kinases such as EPHA2 and DDR1, SRC kinase, and transcriptional regulators including TBX3, ETV5 and TFAP2C set where a duct branches and where branching is suppressed.

Androgen receptor signaling drives male sexual differentiation, spermatogenesis, muscle and bone anabolism, and the growth of prostate epithelium; tuning its output is what these genes do, and their failure underlies androgen insensitivity at one extreme and castration-resistant prostate cancer at the other. Most act as coregulators recruited to the receptor at hormone-responsive promoters: acetyltransferase and deacetylase activities such as EP300, HDAC1 and SIRT1, the demethylases KDM1A and KDM4C, corepressor scaffolds NCOR1 and NCOR2, and the chromatin remodeller SMARCA4 set whether a target gene is switched on or held silent. Others modulate receptor abundance, stability or localisation through ubiquitin ligases and SUMO pathways, or through kinase input. Growth factor and Wnt-related components add crosstalk, so hormone sensitivity is set jointly by endocrine and local signals rather than by ligand concentration alone.

Although framed as control over the extent of cell growth, the genes here describe how neurons set and limit the size of their outgrowths — axon and dendrite extension, growth cone advance, and the decision to stop. This determines wiring during development and constrains regrowth after injury, where inhibitory cues make the difference between a repaired and a permanently severed tract. Guidance ligands and their receptors — semaphorins with plexins and neuropilin, netrin with DCC, slits, ephrins with EPH receptors — converge on Rho-family GTPase signalling through PAK1 and LIMK1 to remodel actin, while MAP1B, MAPT, CLASP2 and tubulin-modifying activity govern microtubule invasion of the growth cone. Trophic input from NGF, BDNF and their receptors, plus WNT and GSK3B, biases growth toward extension, whereas myelin-associated MAG and RTN4 acting through RTN4R impose the collapse and stalling that caps outgrowth.

Where a cell puts its microtubule organizing center determines the axis along which it divides, migrates, or builds a cilium, and this pathway covers the positioning and anchoring of that center. Positioning the centrosome or nucleus-associated MTOC underlies spindle orientation in dividing epithelium and neural progenitors, centrosome migration to the apical surface during ciliogenesis, and nuclear movement in migrating and differentiating cells. Dynein and kinesin motors with their adaptors and regulators — including LIS1, NDE1 and NDEL1, BICD2 and KIF5B — pull on astral microtubules, while LINC complex components SUN1, SUN2 and the nesprins SYNE1/SYNE2 couple the cytoskeleton across the nuclear envelope. Scaffolds and cortical cues such as AKAP9, ninein, GPSM2, DLG1 and ezrin fix the attachment site. Loss of these functions produces microcephaly, lissencephaly and other neurodevelopmental and ciliopathy phenotypes.

N-acylethanolamines are lipid signalling molecules — among them anandamide, the endocannabinoid, and the anti-inflammatory mediators palmitoylethanolamide and oleoylethanolamide — and this pathway covers how they are made and destroyed. Their turnover sets the tone of cannabinoid receptor and PPAR-alpha signalling, and thereby influences pain thresholds, appetite and feeding behaviour, neuronal excitability and the resolution of inflammation. Synthesis begins with membrane N-acylphosphatidylethanolamines, which a dedicated phospholipase D releases directly as N-acylethanolamines; a parallel route proceeds through glycerophospho-N-acylethanolamine intermediates hydrolysed by glycerophosphodiesterases such as GDE1, GDPD1 and GDPD3. Degradation limits signalling duration, with the lysosomal amidase NAAA preferentially hydrolysing palmitoylethanolamide in macrophages and other immune cells. Because these lipids are produced on demand rather than stored, the balance between the synthetic and hydrolytic arms determines local signal strength, and NAAA blockade is pursued as a non-opioid analgesic strategy.

Vitamin D acts as a hormone, and its effects on calcium and phosphate handling, bone mineralisation, epithelial differentiation and immune tone all depend on how strongly its nuclear receptor drives transcription. Regulation of vitamin D receptor signalling sets that gain. Ligand supply is one control point: the renal 1alpha-hydroxylase CYP27B1 converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to the active 1,25-dihydroxy form that binds the receptor. Downstream, VDR partners with retinoid X receptors and recruits coactivators such as MED1, SNW1 and TRIM24 to target promoters, while corepressor-associated factors including KANK2, MN1 and the transcription factor SNAI2 restrain or redirect the response. Tuning this axis determines intestinal calcium absorption and parathyroid feedback; loss of ligand production or receptor responsiveness produces rickets and osteomalacia, and altered coregulator balance shifts vitamin D-dependent growth control in epithelia.

Cadmium enters cells opportunistically through transporters built for essential metals such as zinc, manganese and iron, and once inside it displaces those metals from enzymes and drives oxidative injury to kidney, lung and bone. Detoxification of cadmium ion is the set of buffering and transport steps that keep free intracellular cadmium low, either by chelating it or by moving it out of the cytosol into vesicular compartments or across the plasma membrane. A metallothionein provides thiol-rich, high-affinity binding that sequesters the metal, while zinc and divalent-metal carriers of the SLC30, SLC39 and SLC11 families and the ABC transporter ABCB6 determine how much cadmium is taken up or effluxed. The same proteins therefore couple heavy-metal handling to normal zinc and manganese homeostasis, and variation in them shapes individual susceptibility to dietary and tobacco cadmium exposure.

The nephric duct is the tube that drains the primitive kidney, and its initial formation sets up the plumbing from which the ureter, collecting system and, in males, parts of the reproductive tract derive. Epithelialisation of the intermediate mesoderm into a patent duct that extends caudally to insert into the cloaca depends on a small transcriptional and signalling module: PAX2 and GATA3 specify and maintain the nephric duct epithelium and guide its caudal extension, HNF1B shapes tubular epithelial identity, and BMP4 and WNT9B provide the surrounding instructive signals, with WNT9B later inducing metanephric mesenchyme. Failure or misrouting at this stage produces congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract, including renal agenesis, duplex or ectopic ureters and vesicoureteral reflux, and mutations in these regulators cause inherited renal-coloboma and renal cyst syndromes.

Some viruses pack two genes into one messenger RNA and get both translated by letting the ribosome restart rather than reload. In this termination-reinitiation strategy, ribosomes finish the upstream open reading frame, but instead of dissociating completely a fraction of 40S subunits stay tethered to the message and resume initiation at the downstream start codon, so a single dicistronic transcript yields two proteins in fixed proportion. The tethering depends on subunits of the eIF3 complex, the large multisubunit initiation factor that normally binds the 40S subunit and coordinates mRNA and initiator tRNA recruitment; a short upstream RNA element near the stop codon holds eIF3-bound ribosomes in place. This gives viruses such as caliciviruses and influenza B a way to control the stoichiometry of structural and accessory proteins without additional promoters or subgenomic RNAs, exploiting host initiation machinery for gene expression the cell would not otherwise permit.

Superoxide is both a weapon and a hazard, and this regulatory programme sets how much of it a cell makes and how fast it is disposed of. Tight control matters in two settings above all: the phagocyte respiratory burst that kills ingested microbes, and vascular and neuronal tissue, where excess superoxide oxidises lipids and proteins and drives inflammation, hypertension and neurodegeneration. Control is exerted at several levels — assembly and activation of the NADPH oxidase, with CYBA as a core membrane subunit and receptors such as CD36, CLEC7A, FPR2 and integrin CD11b/CD18 feeding through SYK, TYROBP and protein kinase C isoforms to trigger the burst; cofactor supply, where GCH1 governs tetrahydrobiopterin and thereby whether nitric oxide synthase produces NO or superoxide; and removal and antioxidant defence via SOD1 and NRF2-driven gene expression. Angiotensinogen, TGF-β1 and amyloid precursor protein link the pathway to hormonal and degenerative contexts.

The nervous system is built and later replenished from a reserve of undifferentiated progenitors, and neuronal stem cell population maintenance is the set of processes that keeps that reserve intact rather than letting it differentiate away. Its balance sets brain size and the supply of neurons for hippocampal and olfactory neurogenesis; premature exhaustion depletes the niche, while excess self-renewal favours tumour growth. Notch signalling through NOTCH1 with the DLL1 and JAG1 ligands sustains the undifferentiated state via the HES1 and HES5 repressors, SOX2 and REST hold neural genes in a progenitor-appropriate configuration, and FOXO3 limits oxidative stress in quiescent cells. Adherens junctions built on CDH2 anchor progenitors in the ventricular zone, and centrosomal and spindle proteins such as ASPM, MCPH1 and PCM1 orient divisions, with their loss producing microcephaly from a prematurely spent progenitor pool.

Amelogenesis is how ameloblasts build tooth enamel, the hardest tissue in the body, in two phases: a secretory stage in which a protein-rich matrix is laid down and crystallites elongate, and a maturation stage in which that matrix is degraded and replaced by dense mineral. Amelogenin and enamelin form the scaffold, the proteases MMP20 and KLK4 remove it on schedule, and FAM20A and FAM20C control secretory-pathway phosphorylation of matrix proteins. Mineralization demands sustained ion movement and pH buffering across the ameloblast, supplied by calcium transport, bicarbonate and chloride handling, store-operated calcium entry through STIM1, and proton pumping. Mutations across these steps cause amelophobic enamel defects — amelogenesis imperfecta with hypoplastic or hypomineralized enamel, sometimes alongside kidney, skeletal or neurological features — making this a paradigm for matrix-mediated biomineralization and for the transcriptional control of an epithelial secretory lineage.

Many cytokines, hormones and growth factors act on cells by routing their signal through STAT transcription factors, and this cell surface receptor signalling via STAT is the route by which immune polarisation, haematopoiesis, growth and metabolic status are translated into changed gene expression. Ligands and their receptors here span the interleukins, interferons, growth hormone, prolactin, erythropoietin, thrombopoietin and leptin; receptor engagement activates associated Janus kinases (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2), which phosphorylate STAT1 through STAT6, driving dimerisation, nuclear import and target promoter binding with coactivators such as EP300. Feedback and restraint are built in: SOCS and CISH proteins, PIAS1, and phosphatases including PTPN2 and PTPRC terminate the response, and several microRNAs tune it. Loss of individual components produces immunodeficiency, growth hormone insensitivity or defective antiviral defence, while constitutive STAT activity, particularly STAT3 and STAT5, supports leukaemias and solid tumour inflammation.

Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by runaway peroxidation of polyunsaturated membrane lipids rather than by caspases. It shapes tumour suppression, ischaemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration and the vulnerability of therapy-resistant cancer cells, which is why drugs that trigger it are of interest. The balance is set by supply and defence: the cystine/glutamate antiporter light chain SLC7A11 feeds cysteine into glutathione synthesis so that GPX4 can reduce lipid hydroperoxides, while AIFM2/FSP1 provides a parallel, glutathione-independent radical-trapping route. On the other side, ACSL4 loads polyunsaturated fatty acids into phospholipids and makes membranes oxidizable, and labile iron released via heme oxygenase or held by ferritin determines how much radical chemistry follows. NFE2L2 and its targets, together with autophagic turnover of ferritin, tune sensitivity, and NINJ1-dependent membrane rupture links the death to release of intracellular contents and inflammation.

Aerobic metabolism constantly leaks superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, and cellular oxidant detoxification is the set of reactions that removes them before they oxidise lipids, proteins and DNA. It sets the redox tone in which signalling, proliferation and inflammation occur; its failure produces oxidative damage linked to neurodegeneration, ischaemic injury, ageing and tumour promotion. Superoxide dismutases convert superoxide to peroxide in cytosol, mitochondria and extracellular space, and catalase, glutathione peroxidases and peroxiredoxins then reduce peroxides, with thioredoxin, thioredoxin reductases, glutathione reductase and sulfiredoxin regenerating the oxidised catalysts. Glutathione transferases conjugate reactive electrophiles, several selenoproteins support thiol chemistry, and NFE2L2 drives transcription of many of these defences. Haem and metal-binding proteins sequester the iron and copper that would otherwise catalyse radical formation, while peroxidases such as MPO and TPO use peroxide productively in host defence and hormone synthesis.

Dendritic spines are built on actin, and remodelling that actin at the postsynaptic side is how synapses change shape and strength. Organization of the postsynaptic actin cytoskeleton underlies spine formation, enlargement and retraction, and therefore the structural component of long-term potentiation and depression; when it is dysregulated, spine density and cognitive function suffer, as seen in intellectual disability and neurodegenerative conditions. Actin monomers themselves are supplied by the cytoplasmic beta and gamma isoforms, while a Rho-family GTPase and a WASP-family nucleation-promoting factor drive branched filament assembly, and a non-muscle myosin II heavy chain provides contractile force. Adaptors and membrane-linking proteins including drebrin-like protein, ezrin, FARP1 and the endophilin SH3GL2 couple filaments to the postsynaptic membrane, receptor scaffolds and endocytic machinery, tying cytoskeletal geometry to receptor trafficking and synapse maturation.

Cytosolic RIG-I detects viral RNA and triggers interferon production; the genes here amplify that detection, raising the sensitivity and output of RIG-I signaling so that an antiviral state is established quickly after infection. This positive regulation matters because RIG-I sensing sets the threshold between rapid viral clearance and unchecked replication, and it must be tuned upward transiently without provoking interferon-driven autoinflammation. Several members act as cofactors that help load or stabilise RNA ligands on the sensor, including the helicases DDX60 and DHX58 and the zinc-finger protein ZCCHC3, while OASL mimics ubiquitin to enhance signalling and ZC3HAV1 engages viral RNA and downstream adaptors. Ubiquitin-pathway components such as USP15 and TRIM15 modulate the ubiquitination steps that license sensor oligomerisation and MAVS-dependent signalling, and RNA-binding regulators contribute post-transcriptional control. The output feeds into type I interferon induction and innate immune defence.

Before a dividing cell can copy its genome, each origin must be licensed once and only once, and this initiation step of cell cycle DNA replication is where that decision is made and executed. Getting it wrong produces under-replicated or re-replicated DNA, chromosome breakage and the genome instability that accompanies tumour formation. CDT1 loads the MCM2-7 hexameric helicase onto origin DNA during G1, and geminin binds and sequesters CDT1 after replication begins so that loaded origins cannot be relicensed within the same cycle. Once fired, the MCM ring unwinds duplex DNA ahead of the fork, and the polymerase alpha-primase catalytic subunit POLA1 lays down the RNA-DNA primers from which processive synthesis proceeds. The pathway therefore couples origin licensing to cell cycle position and is a target of checkpoint control and of replication-stress responses.

Opsonization is the coating of microbes and dying cells with complement proteins and other tags so that phagocytes can recognize and engulf them; controlling how much of this coating occurs sets the balance between clearing pathogens and damaging host tissue. The genes here build the classical and lectin routes to C3 deposition: C2, C4A/C4B and C3 itself, factor B and properdin for the alternative amplification loop, and the recognition molecules mannose-binding lectin, ficolins and collectins with their associated proteases MASP1 and MASP2. Regulation runs in both directions — properdin stabilizes the C3 convertase to boost surface tagging, while the C4b-binding protein chains restrain classical pathway convertase activity and limit deposition on host surfaces. Secreted phospholipase PLA2G5 contributes by modifying bacterial membranes. Loss of these components predisposes to pyogenic and meningococcal infection and to impaired clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic debris.

Removing introns from pre-mRNA begins with committing the spliceosome to a particular branch point, and U2-type prespliceosome assembly is that commitment step. Here the U2 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein is loaded onto the intron branch site adjacent to the already-bound 5' splice site, forming the ATP-dependent A complex that defines which intron will be excised and therefore which protein isoform a gene produces. The Sm core proteins provide the shared snRNP scaffold, SNRPA1 and SNRPB2 give U2 its identity, and the multisubunit SF3A and SF3B complexes clamp the RNA duplex, with SF3B1 and PHF5A forming the pocket that recognises the branch adenosine. DEAD-box helicases such as DDX46 and DDX42 supply the remodelling needed for stable engagement. Mutations in SF3B1 and PHF5A are recurrent drivers in myelodysplastic syndromes and other cancers, where mis-set branch points generate aberrant transcripts.

Absorptive epithelial cells of the gut and kidney tubule display a dense apical brush border, and this pathway drives the positive regulation of microvillus assembly that builds it, expanding the surface available for nutrient uptake and transport. The small GTPase RAP2A, loaded by its exchange factors RAPGEF2 and RAPGEF6, relays apical cues to Ste20-family kinases: STK26 (MST4) phosphorylates ezrin to link the plasma membrane to the underlying actin bundle, while the related kinase TNIK contributes to cytoskeletal remodelling beneath the apical surface. The net effect is polarized actin core formation and elongation of microvilli at the right membrane domain. Loss of signalling through this axis flattens the brush border and impairs the absorptive capacity of the epithelium, connecting Rap GTPase signalling to apical polarity, actin organization and epithelial differentiation.

Purine bases such as adenine, hypoxanthine and guanine are largely insoluble in lipid and must be carried across membranes by dedicated transporters before cells can reuse them through salvage pathways rather than paying the cost of de novo synthesis. This transport activity supplies substrate for nucleotide pools in tissues with limited synthetic capacity, and it governs how effectively nucleoside and nucleobase analogue drugs enter cells. Two families dominate: sodium-coupled concentrative carriers that accumulate substrate against a gradient, and equilibrative carriers that move it down one bidirectionally, with an equilibrative family member also setting extracellular adenosine levels and the tone of adenosine receptor signalling. An additional facilitative carrier acts as the main nucleobase-preferring route, and a glycerol-permeable aquaporin channel contributes further purine permeability. Loss of function in this group causes lysosomal and immune disorders and alters chemotherapy and antiviral drug uptake.

Lymphocytes only work if they reach the right tissue, and this pathway covers the signals that increase their movement out of blood and through lymphoid organs and inflamed sites. It underlies immune surveillance, germinal centre organisation and the recruitment of T and B cells to infection or tumour, and its dysregulation drives chronic inflammatory and autoimmune infiltration. Chemokines and their receptors set the direction: CXCL12, CXCL13 and CCL21 guide homing to lymphoid niches, while CCL3, CCL5, CXCL10 and CCR2 dominate inflammatory recruitment. Adhesion and endothelial junction molecules including ITGA4, MADCAM1 and JAM2 mediate arrest and diapedesis, particularly gut homing. Inside the cell, RHOA, DOCK8, PTK2B, NEDD9 and the WNK1–OXSR1/STK39 kinase module control cytoskeletal polarity, volume regulation and motility, and ADAM proteases shed surface receptors to tune the response.

MicroRNAs are not permanent once made; their lifetime is actively set, and this pathway covers the controls on miRNA degradation. Because a miRNA's repressive output scales with its abundance, tuning turnover shifts whole programmes of target gene expression during development, differentiation and inflammatory responses. Several routes appear here: ZSWIM8 acts as the substrate receptor of a ubiquitin ligase that destroys Argonaute proteins engaged by particular targets, triggering decay of the bound miRNA; TENT2 adds untemplated nucleotides to small RNA 3' ends, altering stability; PNPT1 is a phosphorolytic exoribonuclease; and ZC3H12A degrades inflammatory transcripts and interacts with miRNA processing. RNA-binding proteins such as LIN28B and QKI, and long noncoding RNAs including NEAT1 and HOTTIP, modulate the availability and fate of specific small RNAs. Dysregulated miRNA clearance contributes to failures of developmental timing and to tumour progression.

Cellular senescence is a permanent exit from the cell cycle imposed on damaged, stressed or oncogene-expressing cells, and the regulation of that decision determines whether a cell is arrested, killed, or allowed to keep dividing. Too little restraint contributes to tumour suppression failure; too much drives tissue ageing and the inflammatory secretory state of accumulated senescent cells. Control is exerted at several levels: telomere maintenance by telomerase and telomere-binding proteins sets replicative limits, the p53 axis and PTEN-PI3K signalling relay damage and growth cues, CDK6 and RBL1 act on the arrest machinery itself, and SIRT1, SIRT6 and the histone methyltransferase SUV39H1 impose chromatin changes that lock in the state. Cytosolic DNA sensing through CGAS links genome damage to inflammatory output, while numerous microRNAs tune the threshold. Prelamin A processing by ZMPSTE24 ties this to premature ageing syndromes.

Interferon gamma, released mainly by T cells and NK cells, converts responding cells into an antimicrobial and antigen-presenting state, and the genes it induces define that state. The response underlies clearance of intracellular bacteria, protozoa and viruses, drives tumour immune recognition, and when chronic contributes to autoimmunity, macrophage activation syndromes and immune checkpoint-mediated escape. Receptor engagement signals through JAK2 and STAT1 with IRF1 and IRF9 amplifying transcription, raising class I and class II MHC together with the peptide-loading machinery TAP1, TAPBP and the immunoproteasome subunits PSMB8 and PSMB9, and CIITA and NLRC5 as the transactivators that coordinate them. Downstream products include chemokines CXCL9, CXCL10 and CXCL11 that recruit lymphocytes, adhesion molecules, complement components, guanylate-binding proteins, IDO1-mediated tryptophan depletion, nucleic acid sensors, apoptotic effectors, and PD-L1 plus SOCS1 as brakes limiting the response.

Interferons do more than announce infection: through JAK cSTAT signalling they switch on hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes whose products attack viruses directly, and this is the effector arm of that response. Cells lacking it fail to restrict viral replication despite intact sensing, while excessive or unchecked activity drives interferonopathy and autoinflammation. Several distinct mechanisms are represented. Double-stranded RNA activates PKR, which phosphorylates the translation initiation factor eIF2α and shuts down protein synthesis, and the oligoadenylate synthetases, which generate second messengers that unleash RNase L to degrade RNA; the IFIT proteins sequester viral transcripts from the initiation machinery, MX1 and MX2 trap incoming nucleocapsids, and guanylate-binding proteins target intracellular pathogens. ISG15 is conjugated to substrates by a dedicated E1 cE2 cE3 cascade and removed by USP18, which also restrains further interferon signalling. Nuclear pore and cytoskeletal components reflect the trafficking steps these effectors intercept.

Several secreted proteins acquire calcium-binding ability only after a vitamin K-dependent modification made as they transit the secretory pathway. Gamma-carboxylation converts glutamate residues in an amino-terminal Gla motif into gamma-carboxyglutamate, which lets the mature protein bind calcium and dock onto membrane phospholipid surfaces; removal of the propeptide by a furin-type protease in the Golgi completes maturation. Most of the substrates run the coagulation cascade and its brakes — prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X, together with the anticoagulant proteins C, S and Z — so loss of the carboxylase or of its vitamin K cofactor produces bleeding disorders, and this chemistry is the target of warfarin-class anticoagulants. Other clients extend the theme beyond haemostasis: osteocalcin in bone mineralization and Gas6 in receptor tyrosine kinase signalling and apoptotic cell clearance.

Newly initiated RNA polymerase II transcripts are capped while still being made, and this step links the polymerase to the capping enzymes during transcription of the integrated HIV provirus. Capping protects the nascent 5' end from exonucleases and marks the transcript for export and translation, so viral mRNAs depend on it as host mRNAs do. The mechanism runs through the heptapeptide repeats of the largest polymerase subunit: the TFIIH-associated kinase CDK7, with its cyclin H and MNAT1 partners, phosphorylates serine 5 of the C-terminal domain near the promoter, and the phosphorylated tail is bound directly by the guanylyltransferase and the cap methyltransferase, which stimulates guanylyl transfer. The elongation factor SPT5 contributes to coupling capping with early elongation. This phosphorylation mark is the timing signal that restricts capping to polymerase II products.

TLR10 is an innate immune receptor of the Toll-like family expressed in a restricted way, mainly on B cells and dendritic cells, whose ligands remain poorly defined; it homodimerizes and can pair with TLR1 and TLR2, and signals through the MyD88 adaptor. The downstream cascade described here is the shared MyD88-dependent route that converts receptor engagement into inflammatory gene expression: IRAK4, IRAK1/2 and Pellino ligases assemble with TRAF6 and the TAK1-TAB complex, K63-linked ubiquitin chains built by UBE2N/UBE2V1 relay the signal, and the IKK complex frees NF-kB from IkB while parallel MAP kinase branches activate p38, JNK, ERK and the AP-1, CREB, ELK1 and MEF2 transcription factors. DUSP phosphatases, PP2A subunits and deubiquitinases restrain the output. The result is cytokine production and antigen-presenting cell activation; TLR10 itself is generally regarded as a dampener of inflammatory TLR responses.

Influenza virus encodes no ribosomes of its own, so every viral protein is made by the host translation apparatus; this step converts spliced and unspliced viral mRNA in the cytoplasm into the roughly ten polypeptides that build new particles, including the surface glycoproteins HA and NA, the polymerase subunits PB1, PB2 and PA, nucleoprotein, matrix proteins and NS1. The bulk of the gene content is the cytoplasmic 40S and 60S ribosomal subunit proteins that carry out initiation and elongation. Conserved viral 5' untranslated sequences favour recruitment of this machinery, aided by the host G-rich sequence factor GRSF1, while the co-chaperone P58(IPK) restrains the antiviral kinase PKR so that initiation is not shut down by the interferon-induced translational block. Host protein synthesis falls at the same time, making this the point where the virus captures a central cellular process to its own ends.

Neurons are eliminated during development and after injury when the p75 neurotrophin receptor, rather than TrkA, dominates the response to nerve growth factor or its unprocessed precursor, and this receptor-initiated death programme is what the intracellular adaptors NRAGE, NRIF and NADE carry forward. It matters because it sculpts the size of neuronal populations to match their targets and contributes to neuronal loss after axotomy and in degenerative injury. Ligand-bound NGFR recruits TRAF6 and MAGED1 (NRAGE), engages Rac1 through an array of Rho-family exchange factors, and activates JNK, converging on BAD, BIM and caspase-3 to dismantle the cell. In parallel, gamma-secretase components including presenilins and nicastrin cleave the receptor so that its intracellular domain, with NRIF, can reach the nucleus and drive transcriptional events; ubiquitin and SQSTM1 support the signalling scaffold.

Nudix hydrolases keep the cellular nucleotide pool clean, and the phosphate bond hydrolysis they carry out is best understood as sanitation: damaged or surplus nucleotides are cleaved before they can be used as substrates. Oxidised, deaminated or methylated purine nucleoside di- and triphosphates are degraded by enzymes such as NUDT1, NUDT15 and NUDT18, preventing their incorporation into DNA as mutations or into mRNA as mistranslated protein. NUDT16 acts on inosine- and other modified guanine-containing nucleotides, while NUDT9 and NUDT5 hydrolyse ADP-ribose, limiting non-enzymatic ADP-ribosylation of proteins and the accumulation of a potent second messenger; ADPRM degrades ADP-ribose 1''-phosphate from tRNA splicing. Because these enzymes also destroy nucleotide analogues, their activity sets tolerance to thiopurine and other nucleoside-based chemotherapies, and NUDT15 variants cause severe drug toxicity.

TGF-beta signalling normally restrains epithelial proliferation, and cancers frequently escape that restraint by breaking the step at which the receptor writes its signal onto its effectors. Ligand-bound TGFBR2 recruits and activates the TGFBR1 kinase, which phosphorylates the conserved C-terminal Ser-Ser-X-Ser motif of SMAD2 and SMAD3 after the anchoring protein ZFYVE9 presents them at the membrane; phosphorylated SMAD2/3 then assemble heterotrimers with SMAD4 and enter the nucleus to direct growth-inhibitory transcription. Cancer-associated mutants of this phosphorylation motif substitute, delete or truncate the critical serines, so the receptor complex can no longer activate them, the heterotrimer never forms, and the antiproliferative arm of the pathway is silenced. Loss of this input contributes to tumour growth and to the switch of residual TGF-beta signalling toward invasion, while leaving receptor activation itself intact.

Reducing power for biosynthesis and antioxidant defence comes largely from NADPH, and this route regenerates it outside the mitochondrion by oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate. Cytosolic and peroxisomal isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH1) performs the NADP+-dependent step, while aconitase (ACO1) supplies its substrate by isomerising citrate exported from mitochondria to isocitrate. The NADPH produced supports fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis, regeneration of reduced glutathione and thioredoxin, and detoxification of peroxides, which matters in peroxisomes where beta-oxidation generates oxidative load. Related NADP+/NADPH balancing in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen sustains reductive reactions there. Because IDH1 also links this chemistry to 2-oxoglutarate availability for dioxygenases, mutations that alter its catalytic output reshape cellular redox state and metabolite-dependent epigenetic signalling, as seen in gliomas and myeloid malignancies.

Extracellular ATP, ADP, UTP and adenosine act as signals reporting cell damage, stress and nucleotide release, and this family of nucleotide-like purinergic receptors is how cells read them. The set covers the G protein-coupled arm: four adenosine receptors that tune vascular tone, inflammation, neuronal excitability and cardiac rate, and the P2Y receptors that respond to nucleotides. Some couple through Gq to phospholipase C and calcium release, others through Gi to lower cyclic AMP, so a single nucleotide can produce opposing outcomes depending on which receptor a cell expresses. P2RY12 on platelets drives ADP-dependent aggregation and is the target of widely used antithrombotic drugs. Related orphan and lysophospholipid-responsive receptors are grouped here by sequence kinship. Collectively these receptors shape vascular reactivity, immune cytokine secretion, platelet activation and apoptotic responses to nucleotide release.

Smooth muscle contraction generates the force that narrows blood vessels, moves food through the gut, and controls airway, bladder and uterine tone, responding to autonomic nerves, hormones, local mediators and stretch rather than to voluntary command. Calcium entry, here through low-voltage T-type channels, loads calmodulin, which activates myosin light chain kinase to phosphorylate the regulatory light chains of smooth muscle myosin and permit actin cross-bridge cycling; a parallel caldesmon-dependent arm modulates the actin filament in a manner analogous to troponin. Because the contractile apparatus is anchored not to sarcomeres but to dense bodies and focal adhesions built on talin, vinculin, paxillin and integrins, shortening squeezes the whole cell. Relaxation runs through nitric oxide-stimulated soluble guanylate cyclase and cGMP, the target of phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors. Dysregulation underlies hypertension, vasospasm, asthmatic bronchoconstriction and bowel dysmotility.

Hedgehog signalling converts a secreted morphogen gradient into patterned gene expression, and it is what tells cells in the limb bud, neural tube and developing skeleton which position they occupy; in adults it maintains stem and progenitor compartments. Loss of output causes birth defects such as holoprosencephaly and polydactyly, while inappropriate reactivation drives basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. Ligands SHH, IHH and DHH are lipid-modified and released, then bind the receptor PTCH1, relieving its inhibition of Smoothened. Signalling is organised at the primary cilium, so intraflagellar transport components, the anterograde kinesin motor, retrograde dynein and tubulins are integral rather than incidental. In the off state, GPR161 raises cAMP and protein kinase A, GSK3 and casein kinase 1 prime GLI proteins for processing by the ubiquitin-proteasome system into repressors; SUFU sequesters them. Activation preserves full-length GLI activators, with SPOP, ITCH and SMURF ligases tuning the response.

Dishevelled proteins sit at the hub of WNT reception, and one way cells set the ceiling on WNT output is by sequestering them. This branch describes negative regulation of TCF-dependent signalling by DVL-interacting proteins: CXXC4 (Idax) and CCDC88C (DAPLE) bind DVL1, DVL2 and DVL3 directly and dampen their ability to relay signal from activated receptors, so less beta-catenin escapes destruction and fewer TCF/LEF target genes are switched on. Because WNT/beta-catenin activity governs stem cell renewal, body axis patterning and tissue growth, restraint at the DVL step matters as much as activation does; loss of CCDC88C causes congenital hydrocephalus, and unchecked TCF-dependent transcription is a hallmark of colorectal tumourigenesis. DVL is also the point where canonical and planar-cell-polarity WNT branches diverge, so its interactors influence which route a WNT signal takes.
