The long plateau that distinguishes cardiac from nerve action potentials comes from a near-balance between inward and outward current, and this phase 2 biology is what keeps ventricular myocytes depolarized long enough for calcium-induced calcium release to drive a full contraction and for the refractory period to prevent re-excitation. Depolarization is sustained by Ca2+ entry through L-type channels built around the CACNA1C pore-forming subunit with beta, alpha2delta and gamma accessory subunits that tune trafficking and gating, and it is opposed by the slow delayed rectifier carried by KCNQ1 in partnership with KCNE subunits that convert the channel's kinetics to the slow, non-inactivating current needed here. The scaffold AKAP9 anchors kinase signalling to KCNQ1 so that adrenergic stimulation shortens the plateau as heart rate rises. Mutations in these subunits underlie congenital long QT syndromes and arrhythmic sudden death.

Superoxide is made deliberately by NADPH oxidase complexes, and small GTPases of the RHO family are the switch that turns them on. When RAC1 or RAC2 loaded with GTP docks onto the membrane flavocytochrome and its cytosolic partners, electrons pass from NADPH to oxygen and superoxide is released into a phagosome or across the plasma membrane. In neutrophils this burst is the chemistry that kills ingested bacteria and fungi; loss of the catalytic subunit or of the p47/p67/p40 assembly causes chronic granulomatous disease with recurrent infection and granuloma formation. In endothelium the same output acts as a second messenger that amplifies VEGF receptor signalling during angiogenesis. Assembly is licensed by phosphorylation, with kinases including protein kinase C isoforms and ERK/p38 MAP kinases modifying the cytosolic factors, and S100A8/A9 and PIN1 contributing to subunit handling. Related oxidases NOX1 and NOX3 are activated through homologous adaptors.

Growth factor signalling through RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK must be switched off as reliably as it is switched on, and negative regulation of the MAPK pathway is how the duration, amplitude and location of that signal are set. Without it, sustained ERK activity drives inappropriate proliferation and transformation, which is why many of these brakes are lost or bypassed in cancer. ERK itself feeds back onto RAF and onto MAP2K1 at T292, priming the PP2A holoenzyme and PP5 to strip activating phosphates from the RAF activation loop and N-terminal acidic region; subsequent phosphorylation restores 14-3-3 (YWHAB) binding and returns RAF to an autoinhibited state. PEBP1 sequesters RAF1 away from its MEK substrates, and scaffolds and modifiers such as KSR1, BRAP and PAQR3 constrain complex assembly and membrane localisation. Nuclear and cytoplasmic dual-specificity phosphatases, many of them ERK-induced, dephosphorylate ERK and stress-activated MAPKs, closing the loop.

Glycolysis is the cytosolic route that breaks glucose 6-phosphate down to pyruvate, yielding ATP and NADH without oxygen and feeding carbon to mitochondrial oxidation, lactate production, or biosynthesis. It is the sole ATP source for erythrocytes and a dominant one in proliferating and tumour cells; inherited defects in pyruvate kinase, phosphofructokinase or triosephosphate isomerase cause haemolytic anaemia and exercise intolerance. Hexokinases and glucokinase commit glucose, phosphofructokinase-1 catalyses the irreversible control step, and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, phosphoglycerate kinase, enolase and pyruvate kinase complete the payoff phase, with several steps represented by tissue-specific isoforms. Flux is set by allosteric and hormonal control: the bifunctional PFKFB kinase/phosphatases govern fructose 2,6-bisphosphate levels, while PKA phosphorylation and protein phosphatase 2A subunits tune the enzymes, and glucokinase regulatory protein sequesters glucokinase. Nucleoporins and nuclear transport components appear alongside, reflecting regulated shuttling of these factors.

Nearly every eukaryotic mRNA acquires its 3' end not by the polymerase stopping cleanly but by endonucleolytic cleavage of a longer transcript followed by addition of a poly(A) tail, and this processing determines transcript stability, export competence and translatability as well as which of several alternative last exons a gene uses. Recognition of the polyadenylation signal by the CPSF complex, with CPSF3 as the nuclease, is coordinated with downstream element binding by CSTF subunits, symplekin scaffolding, poly(A) polymerase and the nuclear poly(A)-binding protein that sets tail length. Coupling to the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain, to spliceosomal snRNP and SR/hnRNP proteins, and to the exon junction and TREX export machinery ties 3'-end formation to splicing and mRNA release, while PCF11 and the XRN2 exonuclease drive transcription termination. Misregulated site choice shortens 3' UTRs and removes microRNA control in cancer.

Base excision repair handles the most common everyday damage to DNA ": oxidized, deaminated and alkylated bases produced by mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, ionizing radiation, lipid peroxidation and inflammatory oxidants. Without it, mutation rates rise and lesions such as 8-oxoguanine are mispaired during replication; loss of MUTYH predisposes to colorectal adenomatous polyposis, and the route is also how uracil and thymine glycol are cleared from the genome. Repair begins with one of several damage-specific glycosylases ": UNG, OGG1, NTHL1, SMUG1, TDG, MPG and the NEIL enzymes ": which cleave the glycosidic bond and leave an abasic site. APEX1 and PNKP process the resulting ends, then either POLB with XRCC1 and LIG3 fills a single nucleotide, or PCNA, RFC, replicative polymerases, FEN1 and LIG1 replace a longer patch. PARP1 and PARP2 signal the strand break and recruit the scaffold, and chromatin and telomere-binding proteins set the context in which this repair occurs.

Insulin's message gets past the receptor only through a docking protein, and IRS activation is that step: the activated insulin receptor recruits IRS1 or IRS2 and phosphorylates them on multiple tyrosines, converting them into membrane-associated scaffolds that assemble downstream effectors. This is what couples insulin binding to PI3K-dependent glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis, and to the Ras-MAP kinase arm controlling growth and gene expression. IRS1 engages the receptor's juxtamembrane phosphotyrosine through its PTB domain, with its PH domain anchoring it to membrane phospholipids, then releases once phosphorylated so that SH2-containing partners can bind. GRB10 competes at the receptor and dampens the output, one of several brakes on the pathway. Loss or serine-phosphorylation-driven inactivation of IRS proteins underlies insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, making this node the main site where metabolic signalling is tuned.

Mitochondria make their own ribosomes, and the 12S and 16S rRNAs at their core must first be cut out of a single long polycistronic transcript of the heavy strand and then chemically decorated. This rRNA processing in the mitochondrion sets the ceiling on how much respiratory chain protein a cell can synthesise, since the mitochondrial genome encodes core subunits of complexes I, III, IV and the ATP synthase. Endonucleolytic release depends on the RNase P-like complex of PRORP, TRMT10C and HSD17B10 acting at tRNA 5' ends and on ELAC2 at 3' ends, with FASTKD2 and RNA granule components aiding folding and maturation. Methyltransferases including TFB1M, NSUN4 and the MRM enzymes, plus pseudouridine synthases, install the handful of modifications needed for subunit assembly. Defects impair mitochondrial translation and cause infantile encephalomyopathy, cardiomyopathy and deafness.

Alanine metabolism in humans turns essentially on a single reversible reaction: the transfer of an amino group between alanine and 2-oxoglutarate to give pyruvate and glutamate. This interconversion links protein turnover to energy metabolism, because it lets muscle export the nitrogen from degraded amino acids as a harmless carrier in the blood while delivering a three-carbon skeleton to the liver for gluconeogenesis, the basis of the glucose-alanine cycle during fasting and exercise. Two alanine aminotransferases carry out the step, one cytosolic and one mitochondrial, both using pyridoxal phosphate. Their release from damaged hepatocytes is why serum alanine aminotransferase is the standard clinical marker of liver injury, and the mitochondrial isoform's activity is also relevant to insulin secretion and hepatic glucose output.

Erythropoietin drives red cell production by keeping erythroid progenitors alive and proliferating, and one branch of that signal works through phospholipase C gamma. When erythropoietin binds its receptor, the receptor dimerizes and JAK2 is activated, creating phosphotyrosine docking sites; PLCG1 or PLCG2 is recruited to the activated receptor complex and phosphorylated by the Src-family kinase LYN, with IRS2 serving as an additional scaffold. Activated phospholipase C cleaves membrane phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, which releases calcium from intracellular stores, and diacylglycerol, which activates protein kinase C. The resulting calcium and PKC signals feed into transcriptional and survival responses that expand the erythroid compartment during hypoxia or blood loss. Loss of erythropoietin or receptor signalling causes anaemia, while gain-of-function receptor and JAK2 lesions produce erythrocytosis and myeloproliferative disease.

Peroxisomes cannot build themselves without first installing their membrane proteins, and class I peroxisomal membrane protein import is the route most of them take. The cytosolic chaperone-receptor PEX19 captures newly made membrane proteins, recognising signals within their transmembrane segments, and delivers them to PEX3 in the peroxisomal membrane, where insertion proceeds without ATP or GTP hydrolysis; PEX3 itself is handled by PEX19 together with PEX16, and both can enter the ER membrane co-translationally so that budded vesicles seed new peroxisomes. The cargoes placed this way define what the organelle can do: fatty acid transporters such as ABCD1 and ABCD3, small solute pores, division factors including PEX11B and FIS1, and the docking and ubiquitin-ligase components that import matrix enzymes. Loss of these steps yields peroxisome biogenesis disorders of the Zellweger spectrum, with failed β-oxidation and impaired ether lipid synthesis.

NOTCH4 is the endothelial-biased Notch receptor, and restraining its output keeps angiogenesis and vascular remodelling in check; loss of that restraint gives excess Notch activity, disordered vessel development and, in mammary and other epithelia, oncogenic transformation. Signalling is shut down after receptor cleavage, by preventing the released NOTCH4 intracellular domain from reaching the nucleus and by destroying it. AKT1-mediated phosphorylation creates a binding site for 14-3-3-zeta (YWHAZ), which sequesters the fragment in the cytosol, while the F-box protein FBXW7 within an SCF complex built on SKP1, CUL1 and RBX1 recognises the phosphorylated fragment and polyubiquitinates it for destruction by the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core and regulatory subunits is represented here. Binding to the centrosomal coiled-coil protein TACC3 provides a further inhibitory interaction. This is ubiquitin-proteasome control of a developmental transcriptional switch.

The fate of a drug in the body — how it is absorbed, distributed, chemically transformed and excreted — determines its dose, duration of action and toxicity, and this collection of absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion steps is where that pharmacokinetic handling is carried out. Uptake transporters of the organic anion and organic cation families, together with nucleoside carriers, move compounds into hepatocytes and renal tubular cells, while ABC efflux pumps including ABCB1 and ABCG2 export them back to blood, bile or urine and set oral bioavailability and blood–brain barrier access. Between the two, cytochrome P450 oxidations and hydrolysis by carboxylesterases generate metabolites that UGT glucuronosyltransferases, sulfotransferases, glutathione S-transferases and N-acetyltransferases conjugate for elimination; thiopurine and purine-handling enzymes such as TPMT, HPRT1 and XDH activate or inactivate antimetabolite drugs. Common variants in these genes underlie much interindividual variation in drug response and adverse reactions.

Blood clotting depends on a relay of plasma proteases and cofactors that converts fibrinogen to fibrin at a site of vessel injury, and this grouping collects the inherited defects of that cascade. Loss-of-function changes in factor VIII or factor IX cause haemophilia A and B, fibrinogen chain mutations give afibrinogenaemia and dysfibrinogenaemia, and von Willebrand factor defects impair platelet adhesion through the GPIb-IX-V receptor complex, whose subunits are themselves mutated in Bernard-Soulier syndrome. Failures of post-translational processing matter as much as the factors: vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation by GGCX licenses calcium-dependent membrane binding, and tyrosine sulfotransferases modify factor VIII and related substrates. The balance runs both ways, since protein C and protein S defects, and gain-of-activity variants of factor V and factor IX, tip the system toward thrombophilia rather than bleeding. Scrambling of membrane phospholipid by ANO6 supports procoagulant surface exposure on platelets.

Complement is destructive by design and self-amplifying, so host tissue survives only because its activation is continuously restrained. This regulation keeps the inherent positive feedback of C3 cleavage and the constant low-grade tickover of the alternative pathway from turning on healthy cells, while still allowing opsonisation of pathogens and clearance of dead cells, debris and oxidative damage. Membrane-anchored and plasma regulators of complement activation work in two ways: they accelerate irreversible decay of the C3 and C5 convertases, as decay accelerating factor CD55 does, and they serve as cofactors for factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b and C4b, the role of factor H, membrane cofactor protein CD46, complement receptor 1 and C4b-binding protein. C1 inhibitor blocks the classical pathway proteases and CD59 caps membrane attack complex assembly. Loss of these brakes underlies atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, macular degeneration and hereditary angioedema; many microbes evade attack by capturing host regulators.

Endothelial cells lining blood vessels continuously read the frictional drag of flowing blood, and how they respond to shear stress determines whether a vessel segment stays quiescent and dilated or turns inflamed and atherosclerosis-prone. Flow is sensed at the apical membrane and at junctional and adhesion complexes: the mechanosensitive cation channels PIEZO1 and TRPV4 admit calcium, activating the calpain-2 protease that remodels submembrane cytoskeleton so cells elongate and align with the flow axis. Steady high-volume laminar flow signals through VEGFR2, ATP-released P2RY2, and adrenomedullin acting on CALCRL/RAMP2 to raise cAMP and activate PI3K-AKT, which phosphorylates eNOS to generate nitric oxide and vasodilation. Disturbed or low flow instead engages integrin alpha5/beta1, PDE4D-mediated cAMP hydrolysis, focal adhesion kinase, and PP2A-dependent YAP1 activation, driving NF-kB-dependent inflammatory gene expression, inflammasome priming, and leukocyte recruitment at branch points and curvatures.

Maple syrup urine disease is the inborn error of metabolism that follows loss of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, the mitochondrial machine performing the second, committed step of leucine, isoleucine and valine catabolism. Without it, branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids accumulate in blood and urine, producing the characteristic sweet odour along with poor feeding, lethargy, encephalopathy, seizures, coma and death in the classic neonatal form; milder intermediate and stress-triggered intermittent forms reflect higher residual activity. The complex is built from an E1 decarboxylase made of BCKDHA and BCKDHB dimers, a DBT transacylase core, and the shared DLD dehydrogenase, and requires thiamine diphosphate, lipoamide, FAD and NAD+. Flux is set by reversible phosphorylation, with the phosphatase PPM1K activating the complex. Because DLD also serves pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, its loss causes broader, lethal lactic acidosis. Newborn screening enables dietary intervention.

Chromatin remodelling and histone deacetylation are usually separate jobs; the NuRD complex does both in one machine, sliding nucleosomes with a CHD3/CHD4/CHD5 ATPase while HDAC1 or HDAC2 strips acetyl groups from nearby histone tails. Assembly of this complex is what licenses that dual activity: a nucleating core of HDAC1/2 with MTA1/2/3 and the histone-binding WD40 proteins RBBP4/7 recruits MBD2 or MBD3, GATAD2A/B and CDK2AP1/2, and paralogue choice at each position generates complexes with distinct targets. Recruitment to genes comes largely through transcription factors and chromatin readers, including Ikaros-family zinc fingers, nuclear receptors, ZMYND8 and PWWP2 proteins, and can repress or activate transcription. The outputs shape stem cell differentiation, lymphoid and neural development, DNA damage responses and metabolic gene programmes such as gluconeogenic PCK1, FBP1 and G6PC1, and its subunits are recurrently mutated in cancer.
